Title: When does generative AI adoption pay off? ethical governance as a dynamic capability in SMEs
Authors: Tahereh Hasani
Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) offers substantial innovation opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), yet its performance benefits vary considerably across firms. Drawing on the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capabilities perspective, this study theorizes ethical AI governance as a capability bundle—comprising transparency/explainability (TE), fairness/bias control (FB), privacy/data protection (PD), and accountability/responsibility (ACCT)—that conditions the innovation payoff from GenAI adoption. Using 218 usable manager responses from Canadian SMEs, we test the proposed model using covariance-based structural equation modeling in AMOS 22 and examine moderation through multigroup analysis with measurement-invariance checks. The results show that GenAI adoption is positively associated with innovation performance, while TE, PD, and ACCT significantly strengthen this relationship. In contrast, FB exhibits a significant negative moderating effect, a pattern consistent with a short-run maturity-stage trade-off in which overly rigid or poorly integrated fairness controls may slow early experimentation in resource-constrained SMEs, even though fairness assurance remains essential for responsible scaling. The findings also reveal asymmetric adoption drivers: green-innovation orientation is the strongest positive driver, whereas carbon-footprint pressure and economic disruption are negatively associated with adoption. Higher innovation performance, in turn, is positively associated with adaptability and resilience, operational efficiency, and revenue growth. Overall, the study reframes ethical AI governance from compliance overhead to a dynamic capability and identifies governance-related boundary conditions that help explain when GenAI adoption is associated with stronger innovation performance and downstream firm outcomes in SMEs.

Title: Investigating the effect of notification deactivation on social media app usage: A longitudinal experiment
Authors: Na Liu, Yi Wu, Yi Shen, Carol Hsu
Abstract: Given the potential effects of social media use on health and productivity, it is important to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions that encourage healthier usage patterns. Drawing on dual-system theory, this study examines whether reducing external cues, specifically through notification deactivation, can shift users from impulsive to more reflective patterns of social media engagement. In addition, we investigate how individual differences in social media impulsivity influence usage behavior in the absence of external triggers. Through a 21-day field experiment, the findings indicate that notification deactivation temporarily reduced social media usage during the treatment period but failed to sustain these effects after the intervention ended. Furthermore, individuals with higher levels of social media impulsivity, particularly those exhibiting strong positive and negative urgency, continued to spend more time on social media applications despite notification deactivation.

Title: Breaking the spiral of silence in social media: The interplay between opinion climates and hardcore user identity
Authors: Wanghao Dong, Weijun Wang, Wenjing Zhong, Yu Tong, Wei Wang, Chunmei Gan
Abstract: Social media comment sections (SMCSs) have emerged as important venues for public opinion formation. However, whether the presence of hardcore users (who persistently express minority views) can mitigate conformity pressure, and how the identity (ordinary user vs. opinion leader) further moderates this effect, remain largely unexplored. Drawing on spiral of silence (SoS) theory, a preliminary study and three online experiments were conducted within a simulated SMCS environment, systematically manipulating the opinion climate (supportive, opposing, or neutral), the presence of hardcore users, and their perceived identity. Repeated-measures ANOVAs indicated that a dominant opinion climate drives attitudinal alignment toward the majority position, consistent with the SoS mechanism. However, hardcore users perceived as ordinary members exerted no significant buffering effect. Crucially, when hardcore users were identified as opinion leaders, they effectively disrupted the conformity process, preventing majority-consistent attitude shifts. Theoretically, these findings extend the SoS theory to information-system-mediated environments by identifying opinion leader identity as a critical boundary condition for the spiral mechanism. Practically, the results offer actionable insights for platform design and content moderation strategies aimed at fostering viewpoint diversity and countering opinion homogenization in online discourse.

Title: Too old for TikTok? Nope! Exploring senior adult viewer’s short-form video platform addiction through attachment theory and socio-technical framework
Authors: Zhenya Robin Tang, Xueyan Dong, Yuxin Tian, Dahui Li
Abstract: The rapid proliferation of short-form video platforms (SVPs) has fundamentally reshaped the digital media ecosystem, engaging users from diverse demographic backgrounds. Contrary to popular belief, older adults are not immune to the allure of SVPs, with a growing number of older users becoming addicted to these platforms. Drawing on attachment theory and socio-technical perspective, this study developed a research model to examine the factors driving SVP addiction among senior adult users. Our results indicate that social factors (lack of entertainment channels) and technical factors (perceived functionality complementarity and perceived recommendation personalization) influence senior adult users’ SVP addiction through emotional attachment with content creators and functional attachment with SVP. The findings of the current study offer implications for theory development in the fields of social media addiction and technology use among older adults as well as practical suggestions for promoting the mental health and well-being of older adults in the digital age.

Title: The impact of generative AI on news believability: A mind perception perspective
Authors: Yang Liu, Junming Zeng, Shan Liu, Lu Han
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into news production, concerns have emerged about its impact on audience trust and news believability. Drawing on mind perception theory, this study investigates how perceived attributes of the news producer's mind, namely, cognitive ability, emotional ability, and intentionality, mediate the relationship between the type of news generator (AI vs. human) and news believability. We adopt a multi-methods approach, combining an empirical analysis of news videos and user comment data from Douyin with two controlled online experiments to uncover the psychological mechanisms. Results reveal an AI trust penalty: AI-generated news is perceived as significantly less believable than human-generated news, primarily because of lower attributions of cognitive and emotional abilities, as well as heightened perceptions of manipulative intent associated with AI news generators. However, this effect varies across evaluative contexts. The AI trust penalty is attenuated in hard-news contexts, compared with soft-news contexts, where audiences evaluate believability through diagnostic content-based cues such as factual accuracy and evidentiary support. It is also attenuated in belief-consistent contexts, where belief alignment activates an automatic acceptance process that reduces scrutiny of the news generator. These findings contribute to research on trust in AI-generated content, mind perception, and news consumption by identifying the specific mental attributes audiences consider when evaluating news and by delineating the boundary conditions under which mind attribution is more or less likely to occur. We conclude by discussing practical implications for AI involvement and disclosure strategies in news production.

Title: Actualized fitness technology affordances: Conceptualization and validation of a measurement scale
Authors: Yafang Li, Michelle Carter, Robert E. Crossler
Abstract: Prior research on fitness technologies has identified numerous affordances that support users’ fitness goals. However, these affordances are often conceptualized as perceived action possibilities and described using inconsistent labels across studies, resulting in fragmented constructs and limited cumulative theorizing. Affordance actualization theory suggests that technological affordances have consequences only when enacted through users’ actions. Yet empirical measures capturing such enactments remain underdeveloped. To address this gap, we developed and validated a measurement scale for actualized fitness technology affordances. Following established scale development procedures, we generated items, refined the scale, and assessed reliability and validity through three rounds of data collection across student, MTurk, and Prolific samples. The resulting four-factor, 18-item scale captured distinct patterns of actualized affordances—self-appraisal, social appraisal, rewarding, and reminding—reflecting recurring, goal-directed actions performed through fitness technologies in practice. We found that the validated instrument extended the explanatory value of affordance actualization theory in fitness technology research and established a foundation for examining how enacted behaviors relate to user experiences, identities, and downstream outcomes across digital health contexts.

Title: Designing away technostress: Digital interface nudges, cognitive effort, and digital mindset in complex decision environments
Authors: Maximilian Valta, Christian Maier, Yannick Hildebrandt
Abstract: Complex digital decision tasks can become obstructive when interface design requires users to interpret, retrieve, and compare dispersed information under ambiguity. Although technostress research recognizes information system (IS) design as a potential mitigation lever, it remains underspecified how concrete interface-level mechanisms shape users’ stress appraisals during interaction without removing objective task complexity. We theorize digital interface nudges, which are choice architecture based interface elements that structure options and guide attention without restricting choice, as a focused IS design lever that can reduce perceived cognitive effort during decision making and in turn lower perceived hindrance technostressors. We test this argument in an online experiment in which participants complete a complex car-booking task under either a default setting digital interface nudge, a salience-framing digital interface nudge, or a control interface. Both digital interface nudges reduce perceived hindrance technostressors relative to the control, and these reductions are stronger for individuals with a higher digital mindset. The study contributes to technostress research by showing how minimal choice architecture based interface interventions can shape how users appraise complexity in structured decision interfaces without removing objective complexity from the task itself. It also extends digital nudging research from behavioral choice outcomes to stress-related perceptual outcomes and identifies digital mindset as an initial user-level scope condition that shapes the effectiveness of interface structuring.

Title: Editorial Board
Elucidating the bifurcated effects of artificial intelligence technostress on customer satisfaction: The role of affective reactions and voluntariness of use
Authors: Siqin Chen, Jiabao Lin, Qinyao Zheng, Xin (Robert) Luo
Abstract: To achieve high customer satisfaction with AI-empowered products, companies need to focus on the undesired effects of AI technostress on customers. However, the current understanding of how AI technostressors affect customer satisfaction remains limited. Drawing on affective events theory, we develop a research model to investigate how AI autonomy and AI privacy invasion affect customer satisfaction through their affective reactions and examine the moderating role of voluntariness of use. Analysis of data from 357 customers who had used AI-empowered products revealed that AI autonomy is positively associated with customers’ positive affect and negatively associated with their negative affect, whereas AI privacy invasion had the opposite effects. Moreover, positive affect was found to be related positively to customer satisfaction, whereas negative affect was associated negatively with satisfaction. The voluntariness of use positively moderated the relationships both between positive affect and customer satisfaction and between negative affect and customer satisfaction. The results also confirmed that positive and negative affect play indirect roles between AI technostressors and customer satisfaction. This study provides valuable insights into the complex interplay among AI autonomy, AI privacy invasion, and customer satisfaction by elucidating the bifurcated effects of AI technostress from an affective reaction perspective. The findings make significant contributions to the technostress literature, further advancing our understanding of the influences of AI technostress from customers’ perspective. Our study also provides practical recommendations for companies to modify and innovate their AI-empowered products and enhance customer satisfaction.

Title: Counterfactual patient satisfaction inference under selective observation: A theory-driven machine learning design approach for online consultation services
Authors: Anfei Xia, Jian-Jun Wang, Jingguo Wang
Abstract: Online health communities (OHCs) rely on voluntary postconsultation ratings, yet more than 90% of consultations in our setting went unrated and observed ratings were positively skewed. Grounded in computational design science research and the elaboration likelihood model (ELM), we develop a theory-driven artifact for counterfactual satisfaction inference under selective observation. The artifact combines ELM-based central and peripheral route features, heterogeneous stacking, and support-aware self-training with latent structure detection and reviewer support diagnosis. Using consultations from a Chinese OHC, the artifact achieves strong predictive performance on observed reviewer labels while substantially reducing inference latency relative to RoBERTa and API-based ChatGPT5.4. Ablation and SHAP analyses show that peripheral route cues are more predictive than central route cues. For silent patients, shift diagnostics, support analysis, and LLM-fused proxy validation indicate that the artifact produces less positively skewed counterfactual estimates and improves alignment relative to the main supervised, semi-supervised, and domain-adaptation baselines. A randomized experiment with 275 participants further shows that when satisfaction scores are highly positive and provide limited differentiation, patients place greater decision weight on review volume when selecting doctors. The study contributes a theory-driven design approach that links satisfaction formation, selective feedback observability, counterfactual inference, and downstream reputation-signal use in digital healthcare.

Title: Software upgrade pricing under valuation uncertainty: The role of consumer learning
Authors: Shuxia Peng, Qing Zhang, Bo Li, Pengwen Hou
Abstract: Consumer valuation uncertainty for software products significantly impacts purchase decisions and software industry growth. Whereas existing literature explores various methods to mitigate consumers’ uncertainty, few studies investigate consumer learning from the previous generation of a software product. Specifically, it remains unclear how a baseline version of the software mitigates valuation uncertainty for a subsequent upgraded version, and what its strategic implications are. To fill this gap, we develop a two-period analytical model to examine a software vendor's pricing and upgrade strategies under consumer uncertainty and consumer learning. Through this analysis, our study provides concrete managerial guidance. First, regarding pricing strategy, we reveal that under certain conditions, the software vendor should implement price discrimination by charging a premium to existing consumers for the upgraded version of the software. Second, concerning market education, we demonstrate that increasing the proportion of fully informed consumers may harm the software vendor's profit. Finally, regarding product design, we find that controlling the upgrade level to ensure a moderate degree of similarity between the two versions can achieve a “win-win” outcome, simultaneously maximizing the vendor's profit and enhancing consumer surplus. This study provides software vendors with valuable and actionable strategies for pricing, market education, and versioning upgrades in an uncertain market.

Title: Sounds good and feels better—how anthropomorphism influences artificial intelligence voice assistant use
Authors: Yixiu Yu, Sisheng Liang, Haoqiang Jiang, Rui Sundrup, Andrew N.K. Chen
Abstract: Anthropomorphic design is increasingly embedded into artificial intelligence (AI) voice assistants (AIVAs) to create more emotionally engaging interaction experiences. However, despite widespread adoption, users continue to express significant concern regarding security-related risks, and the mechanisms through which anthropomorphic cues help alleviate this concern remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on dual-appraisal perspectives and affect-as-information theory, this study investigates how anthropomorphism can shape evaluative processing (i.e., perceived enjoyment, perceived security risk, and discontinuance intention) under conditions of technological opacity and uncertainty in AIVA use contexts. We develop a research model in which anthropomorphism functions not only as a generator of affect, but also as a contextual amplifier that strengthens the evaluative influence of affective experience during security-related judgment formation. Survey data from AIVA users were analyzed using structural equation modeling, supplemented by robustness checks and post-hoc analyses. The results show that anthropomorphism increases perceived enjoyment significantly, which in turn reduces both perceived security risk and discontinuance intention. However, anthropomorphism does not reduce perceived security risk directly; rather, the relationship operates primarily through perceived enjoyment, highlighting the central role of affective appraisal. Furthermore, anthropomorphism strengthens the negative relationship between perceived enjoyment and perceived security risk, suggesting that affective experience exerts a stronger evaluative influence under humanlike interaction conditions. Post hoc analyses further reveal nonlinear affective effects, highlight the importance of voice-specific anthropomorphic cues, and suggest that anthropomorphism may also facilitate habitual engagement through affective experience. Based on our findings, theoretical contributions, practical implications, and future research directions are provided.

Title: Does knowledge proximity attenuate or amplify the impact of credibility signals on knowledge use? Insights from two natural experiments
Authors: Jan Schilpp, Rajiv Sabherwal, Marcel-René Wepper, Hartmut Hoehle
Abstract: People rely on sources with greater credibility when deciding whether to use knowledge. However, the moderating role of knowledge proximity, that is, the perceiver's proximity to the focal knowledge and its source, remains unclear. Prior literature suggests conflicting possibilities: individuals with high proximity may bypass source credibility, as they can evaluate the knowledge at minimal cost or rely on the credibility signal, as they can properly assess the signal. To investigate this, we exploited two natural experiments involving the addition of Information Systems (IS) journals to the Association for Information Systems (AIS) Senior Scholars’ List of Premier Journals and the Financial Times list. Based on our analyses of over 100,000 citations to 1,882 papers over observation windows of up to 20 years using difference-in-differences analysis, we found that papers in FT-listed journals receive approximately 30% more citations overall, while papers in AIS-listed journals receive approximately 36% more citations from proximate (IS) journals than from distant (non-IS) journals. We conclude that knowledge proximity amplifies the impact of source credibility on knowledge use, specifically when the knowledge, perceiver, and source credibility signals are closely aligned.

Title: A stakeholder perspective-based ranking system for assessing the sustainable performance of decentralized applications (DApps)
Authors: Yifei Shuang, Xi Zhao, Hsing K. Cheng, Jian Li, Hong Mei
Abstract: Decentralized Applications (DApps), as foundational components of the Web 3.0 ecosystem, are reshaping digital interactions through decentralized, transparent, and tokenized architectures. Despite rapid growth in adoption and diversity, the absence of a holistic ranking mechanism hinders stakeholders from navigating this complex landscape effectively. Existing systems reliant on singular popularity metrics fail to capture the multidimensional sustainability and stakeholder-driven value inherent in DApps. To address this critical issue, we propose a novel ranking framework grounded in stakeholder theory, integrating the perspectives of five stakeholder groups—customers, financial stakeholders, business partners, employees, and societal stakeholders—to evaluate the sustainable performance of DApps. Our approach leverages an automated data pipeline processing on-chain Ethereum transactions and off-chain DApps metadata to synthesize multidimensional indicators via a graph-structured TOPSIS methodology that incorporates competitive dynamics among DApps. Empirical validation demonstrates the system's capacity to enhance ranking coverage, differentiation among long-tail DApps, and alignment with long-term value metrics. This work establishes the sustainability-centered DApp ranking system, advancing stakeholder-aware evaluation in decentralized contexts and introducing a network-enhanced multicriteria decision making model for the dynamic DApp ecosystem.

Title: Effectiveness of empathetic AI in health management on consumers’ advice adherence: The moderating roles of digital devices and health conditions
Authors: Shuqin Liu, Chundong Zheng, Nianfeng Zeng
Abstract: As emotive artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in various fields, including health management, it is crucial to identify the factors that influence consumers’ advice adherence in this context. Based on the congruity theory and cognitive appraisal theory, this research examines the effect of AI empathetic expressions on consumers’ adherence to health advice, and the moderating effects of digital devices and health conditions. A pre-study and three experimental studies demonstrate that AI empathetic expressions, digital devices, and health conditions interact to determine advice adherence. Specifically, when the health condition is perceived as psychological, AI expressing cognitive empathy in health advice on smartphones significantly increases advice adherence, whereas when AI expresses cognitive or affective empathy on smartwatches, consumers’ levels of advice adherence did not differ significantly. On the contrary, when the health condition is regarded as physical, AI expressing cognitive empathy in health advice on smartwatches significantly enhances advice adherence, whereas when AI expresses either cognitive or affective empathy on smartphones, consumers exhibit no significant difference in their levels of adherence to advice. The observed three-way interaction effect is driven by consumers’ sense of AI emotional support. This research contributes to the literature on emotive AI, digital devices, and health conditions, as well as provides insights for AI-enabled health information systems design practitioners and health management service providers.

Title: Beyond speculation: Explaining the intention to use cryptocurrency
Authors: Pouyan Esmaeilzadeh, Karlene Cousins, Hemang Subramanian, Arun Rai
Abstract: Individual cryptocurrency adoption involves a financial decision-making problem that technology acceptance theories were not designed to solve. Where IS adoption requires users to judge a tool's fit for a task, cryptocurrency adoption requires users to evaluate speculative financial returns, irreversible transaction risks, inclusion benefits, and network externalities in a decentralized environment simultaneously. Recent fintech adoption research has begun to identify relevant drivers. However, it examines them in isolation, offering no integrated framework and no validated measurement instrument that captures the full benefit-risk space. This study addresses that gap through two contributions. First, we develop a theoretically grounded research model in which nine second-order constructs (financial inclusion, transaction convenience, financial benefit, network effects, transaction risk, market risk, reputation, structural provision, and early adopter traits) each make distinct, theoretically justified contributions to cryptocurrency adoption intention. These constructs emerged from a grounded theory analysis of three qualitative studies with 163 informants, providing domain-specific theoretical development grounded in data rather than incremental extensions of prior models. Second, we validate this framework through a rigorous 10-step instrument development procedure across four quantitative studies with 3098 respondents, yielding a fully validated measurement instrument for the field. The second-order model explains 61–69% of the variance in adoption intention across Bitcoin and Ethereum contexts and provides a marginally better fit and richer construct-level interpretability than a third-order aggregation. Our key finding is that financial benefit cannot be modeled as a variant of performance expectancy: it involves a speculative risk-return calculus that only utility-theoretic frameworks can capture. The validated instrument enables future researchers to conduct systematic, comparable research on cryptocurrency adoption.

Title: The effects of AI identity disclosure on user responses: A meta-analysis
Authors: Hao Chen, Mengqi Sun, Haitao Chen, Bailing Liu
Abstract: Research into user responses to knowing AI identity information has expanded in recent years, yet the evidence thus far provided does not paint a cohesive picture. Existing studies report positive, negative, and nonsignificant user reactions to AI identity disclosure, but lack a clear assessment of whether disclosing AI identity is beneficial or harmful overall. Moreover, the literature still lacks systematic empirical accounts of the underlying mechanisms and boundary conditions that shape these effects. Therefore, the current meta-analysis aims to synthesize the literature on AI identity disclosure and test different theoretical explanations for its effects. The analysis covers 98 data sets taken from 62 papers, yielding 262 effect sizes. The results reveal a robust overall negative effect of AI identity disclosure, while emphasizing the importance of considering both individuals and contexts of such disclosures. Moderator analyses indicate that the impact of AI identity disclosure varies significantly across sample types, cultural backgrounds, and experimental methods. Moreover, interaction effects were observed between sample types and experimental methods, as well as between task forms and application scenarios. Furthermore, an empirical test of theoretical mechanisms shows that affect transfer, signaling, and task–technology fit jointly explain these effects. These findings contribute to the literature on AI acceptance by clarifying the effects of AI identity disclosure on user responses and provide insights for both practical recommendations and further research directions.

Title: How doctors’ and nurses’ work-related motivations shape perceived system benefits and resistance to CPOE
Authors: Hyoung-Yong Choi, Mark Keil, Arun Rai, Likoebe Maruping
Abstract: User resistance to information systems (IS) remains a persistent challenge, particularly in hospital environments, which are not traditional command and control organizations. Prior research on resistance to IS has primarily emphasized structural changes (e.g., in routines, power, autonomy) triggered by adopting a new IS and how such changes affect users’ perceptions (e.g., inequity, threat of job loss). Less attention has been paid to how work-related motivations are associated with users’ resistance to newly implemented systems. Drawing on an affordance-informed perspective, we examine how healthcare professionals’ work-related motivations (motivation for quality and motivation for efficiency) are associated with their appraisals of the perceived system benefits of computerized provider order entry (CPOE) and, in turn, with resistance to CPOE. Using repeated cross-sectional survey data collected from doctors and nurses across three implementation stages, we find that perceived system benefits mediate the association between motivation for efficiency and resistance to CPOE for both groups. In contrast, perceived system benefits only mediate the association between motivation for quality and resistance among nurses. We also find that the negative association between perceived system benefits and resistance is stronger for doctors than for nurses in the earlier implementation stages. This study extends IS resistance research by offering an affordance-informed explanation of how the same system may be appraised differently across occupational roles and work-related motivations in a professional healthcare context. It provides practitioners with insights into how to establish an effective CPOE implementation strategy to reduce healthcare professionals’ resistance to CPOE depending upon professional role and implementation stage.

Title: Who will generate buzz for you? Predicting review writers for local businesses and online sellers
Authors: Eunjung Lee, Yang Wang, Huimin Zhao
Abstract: Despite extensive research on electronic word of mouth, few studies predict which existing buyers will write reviews, although reviews are critical for businesses seeking online buzz. A key challenge is identifying features that link a potential reviewer to a specific product. Drawing on two ostensibly opposing social mechanisms—homophily and differentiation—we derive two review-style-matching measures that capture a consumer's tendency to bond with existing reviewers or stand out from them. Rating style matching reflects similarity between a user and a product's existing reviewers in rating tendencies, while topic matching captures similarity in the topics they discuss. We also construct measures of users’ review experience, which interact with review style matching in shaping review decisions. Predictive analytics using data from two platforms show that the proposed theory-driven features substantially improve performance relative to baseline user-level characteristics. On average, AUC increases by about 32% when the proposed features are incorporated. More importantly, the results reveal that review decisions are multi-dimensional: users can exhibit homophily in rating styles while simultaneously pursuing differentiation in topic coverage, and vice versa. Rather than a binary choice, homophily and differentiation emerge as concurrent dimension-specific tendencies. We further identify experience-based conditions under which different social strategies arise, showing that both the depth and breadth of review experience shape review decisions. These patterns extend social theories of online participation by showing that similarity-seeking and distinctiveness-seeking are not mutually exclusive but operate jointly across behavioral dimensions, and they enable more targeted identification of existing consumers as potential review writers.

Title: Information security incidents, market valuation, and supply chain spillovers: Evidence from Chinese listed firms
Authors: Xiong Zhang, Meng Li, Qiping Wang
Abstract: Although information security incidents (ISIs) have been shown to severely degrade firm value, their propagation through supply chains remains poorly understood, particularly in emerging markets with distinctive institutional structures. This study investigates ISI spillover effects on supply chain partners in China, a critical context given China's production-oriented economy, dominant State-Owned Enterprise (SOE) sector, and rapid but uneven digital transformation. Our findings challenge Western-centric frameworks in three ways. First, we uncover the “dual nature” of supply chain partner transaction concentration; while creating baseline vulnerabilities, it also provides incident-specific protection through enhanced coordination. This protective mechanism operates only for SOEs, suggesting that institutional structures transform concentration from risk to resilience. Second, incidents originating internally generate stronger partner spillovers than external attacks, suggesting that markets interpret internal failures as signaling systematic governance weaknesses that threaten business relationships. Third, we provide empirical evidence that artificial intelligence (AI) attention amplifies spillover vulnerability, revealing how AI transitions create new cybersecurity interdependencies that increase partners’ sensitivity to ISIs. These findings extend signaling and network theories by demonstrating how institutional contexts and technological capabilities fundamentally alter cyber risk transmission mechanisms. For practitioners, we highlight that optimal cybersecurity strategies must consider supply chain partner transaction concentration and AI-specific technological interdependence—such as deep algorithmic coupling and intensive data reliance—rather than applying universal risk management principles. AI transition is accelerating globally, and our evidence that cyber risk propagation differs fundamentally across institutional contexts calls for context-sensitive approaches to supply chain cybersecurity governance.

Title: Signal visibility and patient perception: How physicians’ prosocial behavior builds reputation in online health communities
Authors: Muneer Ahmad, Anfei Xia, Jian-Jun Wang, Xiaocong Cui
Abstract: Physicians in online health communities (OHCs) increasingly provide free articles and consultations, yet how these prosocial services contribute to physician reputation remains unclear. Drawing on signaling theory, we develop a dual-pathway model that distinguishes an attention pathway through physician visibility from a perception pathway through patient evaluations. Study 1 analyzes 21,368 physician-period observations using a cohort-specific difference-in-differences design to estimate changes in recommendation-based reputation following staggered service adoption. The adoption of free article services (FAS) and free consultation services (FCS) is followed by significant short-term reputational gains, with the estimated gains concentrated among senior physicians and those affiliated with top-tier hospitals. The results also provide evidence consistent with physician visibility as a partial attention pathway. Study 2 uses a randomized scenario experiment with 226 participants to examine the perception pathway. Both prosocial service cues increase perceived benevolence and competence, which in turn predict recommendation intention. FAS exhibits an indirect-only mediation pattern, whereas FCS combines a positive indirect effect through these trust beliefs with a negative residual direct effect. This pattern suggests that more effortful prosocial services may strengthen trust-related evaluations but also generate offsetting considerations. By distinguishing signal visibility from signal interpretation and identifying professional capital as a boundary condition, this study extends signaling theory in digital healthcare. The findings also suggest that physicians and OHC platforms should support visible prosocial engagement while clearly presenting professional credentials and service information.

Title: Unveiling the critical role of ethical leadership in information systems security compliance research: An empirical investigation
Authors: Botong Xue, Merrill Warkentin, Xin (Robert) Luo
Abstract: In the existing discourse on behavioral information systems security, a diverse array of individual and organizational attributes has been investigated regarding the employees’ information security policy (ISP) behavior. However, ethical leadership, a pivotal paradigm profoundly associated with employees’ security behavior, has been starkly overlooked in this domain. The research unveils and examines the role of ethical leadership in influencing employees’ ISP-related behaviors. To test our hypotheses and validate the research model, we conducted a scenario-based online experiment pre-study followed by cross-sectional survey of working professionals. The findings reveal that ethical leadership significantly influences both ISP in-role and extra-role behavior, directly and indirectly, through three mediators: attitude toward security behavior (ATT), subjective norm about information security (SN), and perceived behavioral control over security behavior (BC). This research contributes to the growing streams of information security and ethical leadership literatures and offers actionable managerial suggestions on cultivating ethical leadership to enhance organizational information security performance.

Title: LLM-powered contrastive hierarchical interest learning for cross-platform information recommendation
Authors: Datian Bi, Xue Zhang, Jingyuan Kong, Gongkun Chen
Abstract: With the widespread prevalence of multiplatform usage behaviors, cross-platform heterogeneous data offer new opportunities to alleviate cold-start and sparsity issues in recommender systems; however, they also introduce challenges, such as amplified noise, semantic heterogeneity, and negative transfer. Existing cross-platform recommendation methods often merely share user or item embeddings, thereby creating difficulties in effectively distinguishing commonalities and differences in user interests across platforms; moreover, they lack unified modeling and effective utilization of multilevel interest structures. To address these limitations, this study proposes LCHIL, a large language model (LLM)-powered contrastive hierarchical interest learning framework for cross-platform information recommendation. LCHIL leverages LLMs for cross-platform data augmentation and low-order semantic modeling on heterogeneous graphs to characterize platform-local shallow interests. It then uses a heterogeneous graph attention network to aggregate higher-order interactions and extract platform-global deep interests, while incorporating perplexity-based alignment signals and gated multimodal units to model cross-platform dynamic interests. The framework integrates hierarchical interests into a collaborative contrastive learning process to reduce redundancy and noise in heterogeneous graph information and to mitigate cross-platform transfer bias. Experiments using four real-world cross-platform datasets demonstrate that LCHIL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baseline models on multiple evaluation metrics and exhibits strong effectiveness in alleviating cold-start issues and suppressing noise.

Title: The Dark Side of Artificial Autonomy: Formation and Coping of Relationship-related Technostress between Humans and AI
Authors: Fengjiao Zhang, Zhao Pan, Qian Hu, Yaobin Lu
Abstract: Advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies offer autonomy features that enable artificial intelligence agents (AI agents) to help users complete daily tasks, facilitating the establishment of human–AI relationships. Since users need to balance their relationship development needs for autonomy and relatedness, artificial autonomy may induce relationship-related technostress during the development stage of human–AI relationships, a phenomenon often ignored by prior studies. In the current study, we aimed to explore how the autonomy features of AI agents shape users’ technostress perceptions from the perspective of human–AI relationships and their subsequent coping responses. The results of a two-wave panel survey indicated that there are nonlinear relationships between artificial autonomy and relationship-related technostress. In detail, artificial autonomy has an inverted U-shaped relationship with intrusiveness and a U-shaped relationship with overdependence. For the intrusiveness stressor, individuals are more willing to escape from stressful situations by seeking emotional and physical distance from the stressor (emotional venting and distance from AI) or controlling the invasive technology conditions by engaging in delegation (control over delegation). For the overdependence stressor, individuals prefer to continuously maintain a close relationship with AI agents while reducing stressful experiences, adopting approach coping strategies to modify their attitudes (parasocial relationship) and behaviors (control over delegation) or avoiding emotional disturbance (emotional venting). This study provides new theoretical insights into the impact of artificial autonomy on individuals and enhances the understanding of technostress in the human–AI interaction context. The findings also offer insightful suggestions for practitioners in designing AI agents to better satisfy users’ needs.

Title: The Effect of digital habitus and capital on social presence in online social platforms: a multi-group analysis of facebook and roblox users
Authors: Seoyoun Lee, Younghoon Chang, Christian Fernando Libaque-Sáenz, Alain Yee Loong Chong, Qiuju Yin
Abstract: Grounded in Bourdieu's theory of practice, this study expands the concept of habitus by identifying the interconnections among digital habitus, capital, social presence, and continuous participation intention in the context of social media platforms. Employing a mixed-methods approach combining hierarchical linear regression and artificial neural network analyses, we examined data from 319 Roblox users and 359 Facebook users to explore social presence in digital environments and how distinct dispositions and forms of capital differentiate between users of these different platforms. In particular, this study aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of digital habitus in cyberspace by focusing on the differences between traditional social media and emerging metaverse platforms in terms of the extent to which users operationalize a dual identity, representing a negotiation between their real-world identity and virtual identities in these complex relationships heading toward social presence. In terms of academic contributions, this study develops a novel complex and multidimensional digital habitus concept that surpasses the concept of motivation to also incorporate four different kinds of disposition regarding cross-boundary navigation, transliteracy, augmented experiences, and virtual ownership including non-linear effects. Beyond digital habitus, the findings demonstrate that both economic and social capital exert a significant influence on social presence and continuance intention, whereas cultural capital does not significantly predict user participation. Moreover, the effects of digital habitus are significantly stronger among Roblox users than among Facebook users. In terms of practice, our findings offer insights into designing effective strategies to enhance and encourage user engagement.

Title: Smart services in B2B contexts: A taxonomy and archetypes
Authors: Daniel Heinz, Marcel Fassnacht, Carina Benz, Philipp Luchner, Gerhard Satzger
Abstract: Smart services—data-enabled services built on connected physical products—are increasingly central to digital transformation, yet organizations still struggle to systematically design and scale them in business-to-business (B2B) settings. Prior classifications predominantly reflect B2C assumptions or underrepresent B2B’s multi-actor governance, risk/liability, and data sharing constraints. Drawing on literature and a corpus of 100 publicly described B2B smart service cases, we develop and iteratively evaluate a taxonomy that captures the B2B smart service design space. The resulting taxonomy comprises seven dimensions with 25 characteristics, spanning innovation type, smart service outcome, service provider, target user, analytic capabilities, acting features, and information provision. Building on the taxonomy, we identify five empirically grounded archetypes via hierarchical clustering and qualitative interpretation: (A) Enhanced operational productivity, (B) Retrofitting upgrade, (C) Strategic provider insights, (D) Integrated remote management, and (E) Intelligent autonomous operation. Together, the taxonomy and archetypes provide a shared language for cumulative research and offer practitioners a strategic tool to assess portfolios and plan capability-aligned evolution paths.

Title: The impact of corporate artificial intelligence adoption on labor employment in competitive strategic contexts
Authors: Canjun Chen, Lelin Lv, Changxin Xu
Abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has driven widespread corporate adoption of it to achieve strategic goals. However, the impact of AI on labor employment remains a subject of debate. This study analyzes the effects of AI applications on labor employment within the contexts of differentiation and low-cost strategies from a competitive strategy perspective. Empirical data from Chinese A-share listed companies show that AI adoption in both types of firms reduces demand for low-skilled labor while increasing demand for high-skilled labor. However, low-cost strategy firms exhibit a stronger suppressive effect on low-skilled employment, whereas differentiation strategy firms demonstrate a greater positive effect on high-skilled employment. This phenomenon ultimately leads to significant increases in overall employee hiring in differentiation strategy firms, while low-cost strategy firms significantly decrease their total hiring levels. Mechanistic analyses reveal that differentiation strategies stimulate innovation investments to expand hiring demand, while low-cost strategies reduce workforce needs through cost-cutting measures. Furthermore, the research finds that AI applications generally decrease employee wage levels in low-cost firms while increasing wages in differentiation firms. These findings highlight the crucial moderating role of corporate strategic choice in shaping AI's employment effects, moving beyond the traditional view of technological determinism.

Title: An emotion regulation-theoretic perspective on IS use stress and user resistance during an IS implementation
Authors: Christian Maier, Sven Laumer, Tim Weitzel
Abstract: Knowing that user resistance is a common reason for IS implementation failure, we examine how emotion regulation influences whether IS use stress is transformed into user resistance. We distinguish between two types of IS use stressors, challenge and hindrance IS use stressors, and two types of emotion regulation strategies, cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression. Using empirical data from 185 employees facing an IS implementation initiative, we found clear evidence that cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression influence the relationship between stressors and resistance. We contribute to the IS stress and resistance literature by theorizing affective resistance formation as a preimplementation process shaped by IS use stressors and emotion regulation.

Title: Words matter when gangs cyberbang: Predicting imminent urban violence from gang members’ social media posts✰
Authors: Sherry L. Fowler, Antonis Stylianou, Dongsong Zhang, Paul Benjamin Lowry, Reza Mousavi, Shannon Reid
Abstract: The rise in violent crime across major U.S. cities, fueled mainly by gang members using social media to broadcast messages of loss and aggression, poses an urgent challenge. Although prior research has examined gang-affiliated social media content, there remains a crucial gap in identifying which posts serve as credible signals of impending violence. Addressing this gap is essential for enhancing community safety, improving resource allocation, and optimizing law enforcement strategies. This study introduces a novel research model grounded in a contextualized adaptation of signaling theory. The model identifies key indicators of credible signals, such as follower count, specific hashtags, and retweet counts, which correlate with gang-related aggression. Environmental factors, such as temperature, are also examined for their influence on violent crime escalation. Using this contextualized theory, we designed a machine learning model to predict violent crime counts, training it on a dataset of 143,700 gang-affiliated tweets and their accompanying text and metadata. This approach enables automated identification of credible social media signals related to gang violence. The findings contribute to theory and practice by offering new insights into social media credibility and its link to violent crime, and by demonstrating how such signals can be used for prediction. Furthermore, the predictive model provides law enforcement with advanced tools to anticipate crime and inform community-based prevention strategies and policy development.

Title: The power of language: Other-focused linguistic style and sales performance on home-sharing platforms
Authors: Jinming Dang, Xiang Gong, Chenze Wang, Christy M.K. Cheung, Xiaoxiao Liu, Zhenxin Xiao
Abstract: On home-sharing platforms, hosts write self-claimed descriptions with the differential focus of their attention. Some use a self-focused linguistic style with first-person pronouns (e.g., “I” and “my”), whereas others use an other-focused linguistic style (OFLS) with second-person pronouns (e.g., “you” and “your”). Building on signaling theory and the stereotype content model (SCM), we explore how OFLS influences sales performance. In Study 1, we analyzed 228,078 observations from 33,710 Airbnb listings and found that OFLS positively influence sales, especially for hosts with higher reputation status and properties that appeal to home seekers and business travelers (versus leisure travelers). In Study 2, we conducted a randomized experiment to uncover that OFLS promotes sales by signaling warmth and competence. Our work contributes to the literature by revealing the sales effect of OFLS and provides implications for practitioners to boost sales on home-sharing platforms.

Title: Social media engagement and resource gain spirals: a mixed-methods study of digital empowerment among marginalized caregivers
Authors: Murad Moqbel, Valerie L. Bartelt, Cynthia K. Riemenschneider, Abdullah Albizri, Sam Zaza
Abstract: Marginalized populations facing chronic resource depletion often struggle to access traditional support, yet social media enables new support-seeking behaviors that existing theories cannot fully explain. This study advances IS theory by developing the concept of “digitally mediated resource spirals,” a novel IS mechanism explaining how digital platform affordances alter resource exchange dynamics for marginalized populations experiencing chronic resource depletion, and by providing initial empirical support with mixed-methods evidence. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, we surveyed 251 primary caregivers of children with autism spectrum disorder and conducted follow-up interviews with 16 caregivers. We measured caregiving-related social media engagement as a second-order construct comprising informational and social use. Our findings show that (1) socially excluded caregivers engage with social media despite resource depletion, contradicting Conservation of Resources (CoR) Theory predictions; (2) caregiving-related social media engagement is significantly associated with resource gains across three empowerment dimensions: emotional resource replenishment (power within/well-being), social capital accumulation (power with others/participation), and instrumental resource access (power over resources/support networks); and (3) qualitative evidence reveals how platform affordances and digital-specific resources enable resource-depleted individuals to initiate support-seeking with minimal investment. This research makes three contributions to IS: introducing a portable theoretical mechanism applicable to other marginalized populations and digital contexts beyond caregiving; identifying two digital-specific resource types, ambient emotional reassurance and instant peer validation, extending CoR Theory; and extending IS affordances theory by showing that platform affordances create new resource types and not just efficiently enable existing behaviors. The study also has socio-technical design implications for supporting vulnerable populations through platform architecture.

Title: Integrating e-commerce and social media metrics in prescriptive multichannel retail store efficiency analysis: A case study in do-it-yourself retailing
Authors: Koen W. De Bock, Kristof Coussement, Arno De Caigny, Cristina Ciobanu
Abstract: Multi-store retail chains increasingly introduce online channels that influence the performance of individual physical stores. Drawing on the organized complexity of digital business strategy theory, we conceptualize multichannel retailing as a configuration of interdependent digital and physical capabilities whose performance effects arise through complementarities and cross-channel fit, rather than through isolated touchpoint impacts. Evaluating store efficiency in this multichannel setting requires analytic approaches that account for heterogeneity in e-commerce adoption and digital customer behavior as part of a broader capability system, given a certain store environment. Data envelopment analysis (DEA) is a widely used prescriptive tool for benchmarking store performance. This study extends existing approaches by incorporating store environment and e-commerce metrics as contextual variables in a robust two-step framework. In the first step, we estimate bias-corrected store efficiency scores using bootstrapped DEA. In the second step, we examine how online-related factors are associated with store inefficiency using a semi-parametric symmetrically trimmed least squares regression, which accommodates non-normal residuals and provides a flexible exploratory assessment of environmental drivers. In a real-life case study of 102 outlets from a European retail chain, the proposed two-step approach offers managerial insights into how digital engagement shapes relative store performance for a given store environment and highlights the importance of integrating e-commerce measures into multichannel retail analytics to better reflect the organized complexity of multichannel value creation.

Title: The livestream commerce puzzle: exploring the ineffectiveness of online reviews in reducing return intentions
Authors: Lin Wang, Jiawen Wu, Wenting Feng, Yiran Li, Qihua Liu
Abstract: Livestream commerce has experienced rapid expansion; however, many enterprises struggle with high product return rates. While prior research has focused extensively on purchase decisions, consumer product return intention remains largely unexamined. Unlike conventional e-commerce, where online reviews effectively mitigate product uncertainty and reduce returns, livestream commerce creates an attention-competitive environment that presents a dilemma: Multimodal stimuli divert consumers’ limited attention away from processing online reviews, potentially weakening their uncertainty-reducing effect. Drawing on attentional resource allocation and cognitive dissonance theories, we examine how situational factors, specifically interactivity, time pressure, and the herd effect, moderate the impact of online reviews on product uncertainty. We further examine the distinct psychological mechanisms driving consumers’ return intentions at both the pre-receipt and post-receipt stages. Results from in-depth interviews and two-wave longitudinal survey data from China primarily support our hypotheses. This study offers a process-oriented explanation of how livestream commerce transforms the role of online reviews, shifting the focus from purchase prediction to the mechanism of post-purchase return behavior in multimodal livestream context.

Title: Digital innovation for green transformation: Pressure, practice, and performance of manufacturing SMEs in China
Authors: Hui Peng, Huanqin Ying, Jiajia Zhang, Shouyang Wang, Yaobin Lu
Abstract: Digital innovation triggers great hope for driving green transformation. However, how digital innovation pressures shape practices and how these practices affect firm performance remain underexplored. By embracing institutional theory and the dynamic capabilities view, this study sheds light on the relationship among digital innovation pressures, practices, and performance under the moderating effect of organizational ambidexterity. Using multi-wave longitudinal survey data, our analysis offers three major insights. First, market pressure promotes digital product and service innovation, while government pressure drives digital process innovation. The interaction of these dual pressures facilitates both forms of digital innovation practices. Second, digital product and service innovation exhibits an inverted U-shaped relationship with both economic and environmental performance, while digital process innovation follows a U-shaped pattern. Third, organizational ambidexterity moderates these nonlinear relationships by mitigating the adverse impacts of digital innovation practices and amplifying their benefits. These findings contribute to theoretical understanding and offer practical implications for policymakers and managers of manufacturing SMEs.

Title: Human–machine collaboration and algorithmic decision-making: The role of organizational incentives and AI capabilities
Authors: Anh Luong, Nanda Kumar, Karl Reiner Lang
Abstract: Despite growing investment in artificial intelligence (AI), organizations have yet to realize its potential for complex decision-making. We draw on the absorptive capacity (ACAP) view to conceptualize AI systems as organizational knowledge structures and incentive policies as knowledge transfer mechanisms, examining their effects on human–machine collaboration over time. We conduct a randomized controlled experiment wherein financially incentivized participants evaluate 100 loan applications with AI assistance over 10 decision rounds. Results show AI predictive power and incentive alignment influence organizational outcomes not only independently but also interactively: incentive alignment matters most when AI predictive power is low, suggesting aligned incentives may buffer organizations against the negative effects of AI degradation. Crucially, human–AI joint performance improves as experience accumulates. Further analyses suggest that cognitive capabilities, AI trust, algorithm integration, and decision quality shape individual engagement with organizational ACAP processes. Theoretically, by conceptualizing AI systems as organizational knowledge structures bridging human and algorithmic intelligence through the ACAP development processes, we argue that human–machine collaboration could serve as a new source of learning for organizations.

Title: What roles does leadership play in navigating team faultlines? An empirical study from an online learning platform
Authors: Shouxiang Qiu, Ling Zhao, Xiaobin Zhang, Zujun Shi
Abstract: Although prior research has examined team faultlines in diverse contexts, it remains unclear how faultlines shape interaction and performance in IT-mediated virtual teams, particularly virtual learning teams, and what leadership factors condition these effects. Drawing on the faultline and leadership literatures, we develop a process model of team learning centered on two IT-enabled faultlines: social-dominance-based faultlines and knowledge-based faultlines. We propose that these faultlines influence team learning performance through knowledge exchange, both independently and interactively. We further examine leader support and leader expertise as two moderators representing the behavioral and trait paradigms, respectively. Using data from one of China's largest virtual programming learning platforms, we find that both faultline types reduce knowledge exchange, which in turn weakens team learning performance. We also identify a countervailing interaction between the two faultline types wherein the negative effect of either faultline on knowledge exchange diminishes as the other intensifies. Leader support mitigates the negative effects of both faultline types on knowledge exchange, whereas leader expertise exhibits a U-shaped moderating effect on the link between knowledge exchange and team learning performance. These findings extend faultline theory to online learning contexts and show that leader support and leader expertise play distinct roles in helping virtual teams navigate subgroup divides.

Title: Can only managers enact formal control? The role of team-managed formal control in agile project success
Authors: John Tripp, Vallabh Sambamurthy
Abstract: Although formal control in teams is often conceptualized as manager-imposed, recent literature suggests that teams can enact formal control themselves through codified, mandatory, and repeatable practices. We argue that agile practices such as iterative delivery, retrospective review, and automated testing function as team-managed formal controls (TMFC), distinct from traditional managerial controls. Drawing on configurational control theory and the enabling versus authoritative control lens, we examine behavioral (BC), output (OC), and emergent outcome control (EOC) alongside TMFC and test their associations with agile project success. Using multilevel modeling with 344 respondents across 57 agile teams, we find that enabling controls (EOC, TMFC) are positively associated with perceived solution impacts and TMFC is consistently associated with perceived solution quality. Output control is positively associated with solution impacts but not quality, and behavioral control shows no positive associations with either outcome. We also find a negative interaction between TMFC and BC: When both are strongly present, the positive association between team-managed practices and outcomes is effectively zero, suggesting these control logics conflict when co-enacted. Decomposing TMFC reveals that iterative delivery drives the positive main effect, whereas automated testing is the primary locus of conflict with BC. Team-level, project-level, and subscale-level analyses confirm these findings. Our findings extend configurational control theory by introducing TMFC as a distinct enabling mechanism, revealing the differential roles of specific practices, and identifying a conflict between team-managed and behavioral control not observed with output or emergent outcome control.

Title: The human firewall: Investigating the impact of chronic motivational orientation, message framing, and cognitive constraints on phishing detection
Authors: Junyi Yang, Xuecong Lu, Yuyan Wei, Milena Head
Abstract: Phishing attacks, often disguised as legitimate communications, exploit human psychology to compromise security. Research on phishing susceptibility suggests that the way phishing messages are framed acts as an external motivational cue, enticing individuals to click on malicious links. However, these studies often overlook the role of individuals’ internal motivational orientation and its interplay with cognitive constraints and message design. The paper investigates how a promotion vs. prevention focus interacts with message framing (gain vs. loss), working memory load (WML), and need for cognition (NFC) to shape phishing detection. Across two experiments, we find that prevention-focused individuals exhibit higher detection accuracy for phishing emails but lower detection accuracy for legitimate emails. For phishing emails, this motivational gap is more pronounced under conditions of low WML or among low-NFC individuals, particularly when emails include gain-framed content. For legitimate emails, the gap is especially salient under low WML and when evaluating messages with gain-framed content. Our findings advance phishing research by demonstrating the joint influence of motivation, cognition, and message design, and offer practical insights for personalized cybersecurity training that adapts to users’ cognitive and motivational profiles to reduce cyber risks.

Title: Disclosing AI-generated image or copy? Understanding consumer responses to the AI-generated green advertisements
Authors: Jingwen Li, Lixiao Geng, Yaping Chang
Abstract: As generative AI becomes more prevalent in advertising production, disclosing its involvement is both necessary and crucial for consumers. However, little research has examined the implications of such disclosures in the context of green advertisements. Specifically, it remains unclear which parts of AI involvement should be disclosed in green advertisements to enhance consumer responses when brands use AI to generate associative green advertisements. Through three experiments (N = 632), we found that disclosing AI-generated green image (vs. green copy) increased consumers’ attitudes toward the brand and their purchase intentions for the advertised green product. The psychological mechanism driving these effects is that disclosing AI-generated green image (vs. green copy) enhances consumers’ perception of the brand's environmental claim specificity and authenticity. Moreover, these effects are moderated by the type of mental simulation of ad creation activated in consumers. Specifically, these effects exist when consumers’ process simulation of ad creation is activated but disappear when outcome simulation of ad creation is activated. Our research contributes to the literature on AI disclosures and green advertising persuasion. The findings offer actionable guidance for brands and advertising agencies to effectively disclose AI's involvement in green advertisements.

Title: From large-scale text to model development: A novel approach to algorithm integration in information systems research
Authors: Morteza Namvar, Saeed Akhlaghpour, James Boyce, Marta Indulska
Abstract: We introduce “Seed Word Generation–Abductive Model Development” (SWG-AMD), a method that leverages advancements in semi-supervised topic modelling and abductive reasoning for using large-scale text in research model development. As the efficacy of SWG-AMD depends on quality seed words for seeded topic modelling, we present a novel Seed Word Generation (SW-Gen) algorithm to optimise this critical input. As an illustrative application, we apply SWG-AMD to Australia’s COVIDSafe dataset to build a research model, followed by external validation using two additional datasets. We conclude by discussing SWG-AMD’s utility for researchers seeking to develop context-sensitive research models in high-volume, real-time data settings.

Title: Editorial Board
Communication media choices in interfirm collaborations: When media richness matters
Authors: Constantinos S. Lioukas, Jeffrey J. Reuer
Abstract: Research relying on media richness theory has explored the communication media used by individuals who perform collaborative tasks that involve equivocality, a situation characterized by ambiguous information with multiple interpretations. This research implicitly assumes that individuals have common goals and priorities for collaborating, and so they can expect to encounter only cooperative behavior by the other party. We extend the core ideas of media richness theory to an interfirm collaboration context characterized by mixed motives where individuals can expect to encounter either cooperative or competitive behavior depending on their partners’ motives for the collaboration. In particular, we examine the communication media used during the interactions between alliance managers who are working for different firms with potentially different strategic goals and priorities. We argue that in certain types of alliances, equivocality can affect how partners perceive each other’s motives for the collaboration by leading to two types of errors: unnecessary misinterpretation and suspicion that the other party has hidden motives for the collaboration when in fact they do not (i.e., type I errors) and failing to identify that the other party has hidden motives when they actually do (i.e., type II errors). While unnecessary suspicions can be avoided by using media with higher richness in general, only certain types of richer media can help identify hidden motives. Our findings indicate that alliance managers are not more likely to use richer media for more equivocal tasks on an overall basis, but they are more likely to do so only in certain types of collaborations in which such errors are more likely to arise, and only for certain types of richer media that can help address either type of error (i.e., type I or type II error). We discuss the implications of these findings for research on communication media grounded in media richness theory and research on alliance governance.

Title: Structural or freestyle? How review formats shape review helpfulness and consumer purchase intention
Authors: Chunyu Li, Weiting Chen, Hua Li, Geng Cui
Abstract: Consumers seeking online reviews for purchase decisions are often overwhelmed by information overload resulting from the review explosion. Many platforms offer an innovative structural reviewing format to allow consumers to compose reviews on several product attributes. Through a field study and two experiments, we reveal the advantage of structural reviewing over traditional freestyle reviewing in generating helpful reviews and enhancing purchase intention through the mediation of perceived processing fluency. Furthermore, this advantage is more pronounced for utilitarian (versus hedonic) products, for consumers in an implementational (versus deliberative) mindset, and for novice (versus experienced) consumers. Our findings deepen the word-of-mouth marketing literature and offer important implications for practitioners to capitalize on structural reviewing.

Title: Dual consequences of IT artifact characteristics in reducing sustainable uncertainties: Implications for decision-making within digital supply chain platforms
Authors: Maryam Hina, Najmul Islam
Abstract: Digital platforms are increasingly being adopted for addressing sustainable supply chain (SC) uncertainties. Digital SC platforms, however, have been conceptualized as strategic or infrastructural assets in previous studies, reporting mixed outcomes depending on their deployment and operational focus. Variations in platform design characteristics may explain these mixed findings, especially when addressing uncertainties specifically regarding sellers’ sustainability. However, no prior study has examined how the characteristics of digital SC platforms, namely, immutability, traceability, transparency level, and platform type, individually or collectively impact SC operational integration to alleviate sustainability-related seller uncertainty. We developed a conceptual model to theorize the effect of IT artifact characteristics on SC operational integration and seller uncertainty. We empirically tested the model through an experiment employing a 2 × 2 factorial survey design accompanied by mock-up user interfaces and collected data from 444 SC managers. The results revealed that immutability and traceability improved SC operational integration, subsequently reducing seller uncertainty. However, their effects were inconsistent, being contingent on the transparency level and platform type. Specifically, a high transparency level lessened the impact of immutability on SC operational integration, whereas blockchain-based platforms enhanced the effect of traceability on SC operational integration. Overall, these findings reveal the dual consequences of digital platform characteristics and connecting digital platform design with SC operational integration in a sustainability-specific context.

Title: Understanding the Power of Diverging Voices: Exploring the Interplay of Regulatory Focus, Product Type, and Review Variance on Product Attitude
Authors: Eunju Yi, Do-Hyung Park
Abstract: Online shoppers increasingly encounter divergent product reviews that present both opportunities and uncertainties. Although prior research has examined review variance, product type, and regulatory focus independently, findings remain fragmented and often contradictory. This study offers an integrative explanation by applying the multiplicative structure of Expectancy Theory—expectancy (belief that effort improves evaluation), instrumentality (confidence that evaluations translate into reliable outcomes), and valence (subjective value of outcomes)—to online review processing. We map these components onto three central consumer judgment factors: product type as expectancy, review variance as instrumentality, and regulatory focus as valence. A 2 (product type: search vs. experience) × 2 (review variance: high vs. low) × 2 (regulatory focus: promotion vs. prevention) between-subjects experiment (N = 200) tests whether consumers’ product attitudes depend on the joint configuration of these components. Results reveal a significant three-way interaction: promotion-focused consumers prefer low-variance reviews for search goods but respond more favorably to high-variance reviews for experience goods, whereas prevention-focused consumers consistently prefer low-variance reviews regardless of product type. These findings synthesize disparate prior results by demonstrating that the impact of review variance cannot be fully explained without considering both product evaluability and motivational orientation. The study advances theory by illustrating how contextual (product type, review variance) and psychological (regulatory focus) factors jointly shape consumers' EIV beliefs and, through their multiplicative configuration, determine review-based evaluations across digital consumption environments. Practically, the results offer actionable implications for designing review presentation strategies that align with consumers’ motivational needs and the evaluability of product categories.

Title: Understanding the impact of advertising recommendation sources on consumers' click-through intentions on social media: Focusing on the differences in privacy controls
Authors: Wenfang Fan, Bingjia Shao, Yong Zhang
Abstract: Within-platform and cross-platform advertising recommendations are increasingly used by social media platforms. However, little is known about how advertising recommendation sources affect consumer response under different privacy controls. Grounded in contextual integrity and privacy calculus theory, this study examines how the match between advertising recommendation sources (within-platform vs. cross-platform) and privacy controls (low vs. high) influences consumers' click-through intentions. Results from four experiments indicate that click-through intention is higher for within-platform recommendations under low privacy control, whereas it is higher for cross-platform recommendations under high privacy control. This matching effect is mediated by privacy concerns and perceived personalization, and moderated by consumer risk preference. These findings provide practical guidance for social media platforms to develop effective advertising recommendation strategies.

Title: Information systems artifact as a product attribute: An empirical analysis of the effects of information systems availability
Authors: Yong Liu, Wenjie Fan, Virpi Kristiina Tuunainen, Hongxiu Li, Chee-Wee Tan, Timo Saarinen
Abstract: Drawing from product attribute literature, this study introduces the concept of information systems (IS) availability to elucidate the impact of IS artifacts on consumers and businesses that incorporate these artifacts as product attributes. We contend that the availability of an IS artifact can influence purchase decisions and brand satisfaction significantly. Utilizing the theory of attractive quality alongside two empirical studies, we explore the distinctive performance of IS attributes compared with traditional ones and examine the effects of IS availability on business performance. This research contributes to the IS field by introducing IS availability as a novel concept, thereby enhancing the understanding of IS use and extending existing theories.

Title: From comparison to collaboration: Experimental evidence on human and artificial intelligence in public decision making
Authors: Shangrui Wang, Yuanmeng Zhang, Yiming Xiao, Zheng Liang
Abstract: This study investigates nuanced public perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) in public sector decision-making, extending existing scholarship by examining human–AI collaboration and its various configurations across diverse scenarios. Using a data-centric categorization of decision scenarios and drawing on two experiments in China: a vignette experiment (Study 1; n = 611) and a conjoint experiment (Study 2; n = 894), this study yields two main findings. First, while human decision-making is perceived as more acceptable than AI, AI is seen as more efficient, and human decision-making is viewed as fairer. Notably, human–AI collaboration tends to achieve high public acceptance by leveraging the complementary strengths of both humans and AI across different decision scenarios. Second, the specific configuration of human–AI collaboration significantly influences public perceptions, with collaborative approach, outcome explanation, responsibility attribution, and stakeholder involvement playing critical roles. This study not only provides a data-centric perspective on decision scenarios but also advances our understanding of human–AI collaboration in decision-making, offering practical insights for optimizing its configurations.

Title: Taking control: The impact of question formatting on response outcomes in online technical question-and-answer communities
Authors: Dylan Junluo Chen, Zhewen Liang, Ben Liu, Bofei She
Abstract: Obtaining timely and high-quality responses remains a persistent challenge in online technical question-and-answer (Q&A) communities. While current research has largely focused on platform-level incentives to enhance answerer engagement, the questioner's role in shaping response outcomes has been overlooked. To address this gap, our study investigates how questioners can improve response outcomes through effective question formatting in Markdown-enabled Q&A communities. Drawing upon multiple theoretical perspectives, we examine how question formatting influences the quantity, quality, and timeliness of community responses.
